title: AI Foundations
tagline: Get the big picture without the fog.
description: A 60-card guided run through the core ideas that actually matter.

modules.title: What AI Really Is
modules.summary: The core mental model behind the term.

cards.content: AI is a broad label for systems that perform tasks we usually associate with human judgment, pattern matching, or decision-making.
Not all AI thinks. Most AI spots patterns in data, then predicts or ranks the next likely move.
A calculator follows fixed rules. An AI model learns patterns from examples, then applies them to new inputs.
Modern AI is strongest in narrow tasks. It can beat humans in one lane while failing badly outside it.
When people say AI, they often mean machine learning, which is the biggest engine behind today’s breakthroughs.
AI systems are built by humans who choose the data, the goal, the limits, and the way success gets measured.
A good AI answer is not magic. It is the output of data, model design, compute, and a scoring objective working together.
Many AI products feel intelligent because they are fast, fluent, and context-aware, not because they truly understand the world.
The smartest way to read AI is this: pattern engine first, human meaning layered on top.
If you remember one thing: AI is less a single technology and more a stack of methods for turning data into useful decisions.
Machine learning trains a model on past examples so it can make better guesses on new ones.
The model is not the data. It is a compressed pattern map shaped by the data it sees.
Supervised learning uses labeled examples. The model learns to map input to the right output.
Unsupervised learning looks for structure without labels, like clusters, groups, or hidden relationships.
Reinforcement learning improves through trial, feedback, and reward rather than a direct answer key.
Training is the fitting phase. Inference is the moment the trained model makes a live prediction.
A model can memorize training examples and still fail in the real world. That is overfitting.
A useful model balances fit and generalization. It should learn the signal, not cling to noise.
Features matter. If the input is weak, noisy, or biased, the output usually inherits that weakness.
Great machine learning is not just smart math. It is good data, a clear goal, and honest evaluation.

modules.title: Neural Networks
modules.summary: Why deep learning changed the game.

cards.content: A neural network is a stack of layers that transform input into a prediction through learned weights.
Each layer extracts patterns at a different level, from simple signals to more abstract structure.
Deep learning means using many layers so the model can build richer internal representations.
Backpropagation is the method that pushes error backward through the network so weights can improve.
Gradient descent is the step-by-step optimization process that nudges the model toward lower error.
Neural networks shine when the problem space is complex enough that hand-written rules break down.
They became powerful when more data, more compute, and better architectures arrived together.
Convolutional networks boosted vision. Transformers changed language and sequence-heavy tasks.
The network does not store facts the way a database does. It stores tendencies in distributed weights.
Deep learning feels impressive because it can absorb huge pattern spaces that would crush manual programming.
A language model predicts the next token based on the tokens that came before it.
Tokens are chunks of text, not always full words. The model thinks in token probabilities.
Fluent output comes from strong next-step prediction over massive text patterns.
Transformers let language models pay attention to relationships across a sequence, not just nearby words.
Pretraining gives the model broad language instincts. Fine-tuning or alignment shapes how it behaves.
A chat model sounds conversational because it was trained and tuned on instruction-following patterns.
Hallucinations happen when the model generates something statistically plausible but factually wrong.
Prompting works because the model uses your context as a steering signal for what to predict next.
The model does not browse reality by default. It continues the pattern space it was trained on.
The strongest use of a language model is as a fast thinking partner, not an unquestioned source of truth.
AI inherits the strengths and weaknesses of its training data, including blind spots and historical bias.
A confident answer is not the same as a correct answer. Models are optimized for output, not certainty honesty.
Bias can enter through data collection, labeling, objectives, evaluation, and deployment context.
Even accurate models can cause harm if the surrounding product decisions are careless.
Automation bias happens when humans trust the system too much and stop checking its weak spots.
Privacy risk grows when models are trained on sensitive data or exposed to user input without guardrails.
Robustness matters because models can fail hard on unusual inputs that look minor to a human.
Interpretability is limited. Often we can observe the output without fully understanding why the model chose it.
Good AI governance means watching behavior after launch, not just celebrating benchmark scores before it.
The safest mental model is this: AI is useful leverage, but only when humans still own judgment.

modules.title: Using AI Well
modules.summary: How to turn the tools into leverage.

cards.content: Use AI where speed, drafting, pattern synthesis, or brainstorming creates leverage without high irreversible risk.
Treat the first answer as a strong draft, not the finish line.
Clear prompts improve output because they reduce ambiguity about role, goal, context, and constraints.
Good prompting is less about clever wording and more about giving the model the right frame.
Verification matters most in factual, legal, medical, financial, or public-facing work.
The best workflows mix AI speed with human taste, judgment, and final accountability.
AI is strongest when it compresses effort on repetitive or structure-heavy steps.
It is weaker when the task depends on truth from changing real-world conditions unless external tools are attached.
People who get the most out of AI usually learn how to iterate, critique, and re-ask, not just submit once.
The real win is not replacing your thinking. It is giving your thinking better speed and range.
